overview: This record concerns the Nasrid emirate centered on Granada, not every earlier state that occupied the city. From the thirteenth century until 1492, its rulers developed the Alhambra while households, craftspeople, farmers and scholars sustained a much larger society. The first atlas polygon is 1279; Nasrid rule in Granada began earlier.

periods.title: A new court and growing city
periods.summary: Muhammad I established his court in Granada in 1238 and began the Alhambra’s Nasrid transformation. The growing capital received Muslims displaced by Christian conquests.

periods.title: Palaces, school and hospital
periods.summary: Yusuf I and Muhammad V sponsored major buildings. The madrasa opened in 1349, and Muhammad V’s hospital was built in 1365 to 1367.

periods.title: The late emirate
periods.summary: Nasrid Granada continued until the conquest of 1492. Palace life did not encompass every resident’s circumstances.

items.text: The Alhambra was a fortified city as well as a palace complex. Sultans shared this setting with officials, servants and elite soldiers. Its spectacular royal rooms therefore belonged to a working settlement with many occupations, not an empty architectural showpiece.

Muhammad I’s Acequia Real brought water to the hilltop complex. Channels supported life and cultivation as well as fountains. Keeping a beautiful garden alive required controlling a practical water supply; the view was also an engineering achievement.

The Generalife was an agricultural estate as well as a royal retreat. Its cultivation makes a useful distinction: some green spaces produced food rather than existing only for decoration. The continued garden history after 1492 should not all be projected backward into Nasrid times.

Granada’s Madrasa Yusufiyya, founded in 1349, taught Islamic law and religious scholarship alongside Arabic and subjects such as astronomy, calculation and geometry. These studies helped prepare people for religious and administrative roles. It was advanced education, not a school attended by all children.

The madrasa had resident students, teachers from al-Andalus and elsewhere, and income from endowed property. This shows how learning needed housing and long-term finance as well as books. The institution’s social role changed after the conquest.

Muhammad V’s Maristán served poor Muslim patients. Its surviving foundation inscription dates construction to 1365 to 1367. An inscription and building history provide firmer evidence for this institution than a general claim that all medieval healthcare was either excellent or absent.

The hospital reused an earlier structure and added an upper floor and pool. Its later conversion into a mint around 1499 to 1502 changed the interior. Present remains therefore contain several lives of the building, not a perfectly preserved fourteenth-century ward.

sections.title: At home: light, toilets and toys

items.text: The Alhambra Museum’s household collection includes iron keys, portable lamps and braziers. Such objects helped people lock doors, continue activities after sunset and warm rooms. Their different finishes show that practical equipment could also express wealth.

Surviving hygiene objects include small washing basins and chamber pots used near sleeping spaces. These are evidence for bodily routines that palace photographs rarely show. The collection does not justify claiming that every home in the whole emirate had an identical water supply or toilet.

The museum notes that surviving Nasrid houses do not always reveal a fixed kitchen room. Cooking equipment could be moved to a courtyard or porch. Spindlewhorls, thimbles and needles also point to textile work within homes.

Clay whistles and miniature dishes survive from both the Nasrid and later Christian Alhambra. They reveal play as part of domestic life, but a particular toy needs its own dating before it can be called Nasrid. Children’s noise, apparently, has a long material history.

Some whistles were modeled as animals or people, and some used water to make their sound. The museum distinguishes these types. A small, inexpensive clay toy can tell us something a jeweled royal sword cannot: what someone might have played with.

sections.title: Read a small piece of the palace

items.text: A Nasrid shield tile in the Alhambra Museum bears the Arabic motto “ولا غالب إلا الله”: “There is no victor but God.” The same dynasty’s motto recurs in palace decoration. This is Arabic language written in Arabic script, a statement of royal faith and legitimacy.

The Alhambra’s inscriptions use both angular Kufic and more rounded cursive styles. Some name rulers, while others offer blessings or quote scripture. Writing itself became part of the architecture; different letterforms do not necessarily mean different languages.

ending.text: The Catholic Monarchs, Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon, took Granada in 1492, ending Nasrid sovereignty. The Alhambra became a royal residence under the conquerors, and Morisco craftspeople helped repair it. Political conquest did not instantly erase its people or skills, although their institutions and circumstances changed profoundly.
